# Operating Room Extubation After Cardiac Surgery: A Promising Practice or a Product of Selection Bias?

Chelsea J. Messinger, MD, PhD

,1* Elizabeth Hall, MD 1 Matthew R. Smith, BA, 1 Ariel Mueller, MA, 1 Min Hou, MS, 2 Jordan Bloom, MD, MPH, 2 Carolyn Mehaffey, MD, 1 Lauren Gibson, MD 1

1Department of Anesthesiology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Mass General Brigham, Boston, USA 1Division of Cardiac Surgery, Massachusetts General Hospital, Mass General Brigham, Boston, USA *Correspondence: cjmessinger@mgb.org

## ABSTRACT

Extubation practices after cardiac surgery have increasingly shifted toward earlier strategies, including oper- 1

ating room extubation (ORE), although evidence regarding safety and outcomes remains mixed. On Novem- 2

ber 1, 2024, our center implemented a protocol requiring systematic consideration of ORE for all elective 3

cases involving cardiopulmonary bypass, with prospective data collection through June 2025. Among 628 4

cases, 171 patients (27%) were extubated in the operating room, with a consistent monthly rate of approxi- 5

mately 30%. Patients had a median age 62 years and a relatively low burden of major comorbidities. Rein- 6

tubation occurred in 5 patients (2.9%) and all patients survived to 30 days. Median intensive care unit stay 7

was shorter for ORE patients compared with all elective cardiac surgery patients (25.5 vs 38.2 hours, respec- 8

tively), while hospital stay was similar (5 days). These results likely reflect selection bias rather than causal- 9

ity. Nonetheless, they demonstrate the feasibility and safety of a standardized ORE protocol, supporting the 10

need for a multicenter randomized trial to establish eﬀicacy and define optimal patient populations. 11

INTRODUCTION 12

Extubation practices following cardiac surgery have undergone substantial evolution in recent years. Traditionally, pa- 13

tients remained intubated postoperatively due to concerns regarding airway stability and respiratory complications. 14

Advances in anesthetic techniques, physiologic monitoring, and perioperative care have since facilitated a shift toward 15

earlier extubation—often within 6 hours of ICU admission—and, in select cases, immediate extubation in the operat- 16

ing room (ORE).1 17

A small randomized clinical trial (N=100) conducted in 2018 demonstrated feasibility of ORE in elective, noncomplex 18

cardiac surgery using cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB).2 Several more recent, large retrospective studies have exam- 19

ined the eﬀicacy of ORE. Some report reduced morbidity and shorter intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay com- 20

pared with early ICU extubation.3–9 In contrast, two large database analyses have identified associations between 21

ORE and adverse outcomes, including higher rates of reintubation, longer operative times, and increased in-hospital 22

mortality, though high-volume centers appear less affected.10,11 These findings are limited by residual confounding 23

given the substantial role of provider judgment in determining extubation candidacy—decisions often based on surgi- 24

cal and anesthetic factors not captured in electronic health records or national databases. This intractable confound- 25

ing, combined with heterogeneity of observational studies, highlights the need for a pragmatic RCT. 26

As a preparatory step toward such a trial, our high-volume cardiac surgical center adopted a protocol in which all elec- 27

tive cardiac surgical patients are systematically considered for ORE. Here, we report preliminary safety and outcomes 28

data from the first 8 months of implementation, with the aim of establishing feasibility ahead of a planned RCT of the 29

protocol. 30

MATERIALS AND METHODS 31

On November 1, 2024, we implemented a protocol requiring that potential for ORE be considered and discussed dur- 32

ing the pre-procedural huddle (involving anesthesia, surgery, nursing, and perfusion teams) for all elective cardiac 33

surgical cases undergoing CPB. Prior to this initiative, ORE was infrequent—occurring in approximately 3% of cases 34

in 2024—and many anesthesiologists had limited experience with the practice. 35

Although all elective cases were considered, patients were identified as candidates for ORE during the huddle based 36

on procedure complexity, age, body mass index, baseline mental status, airway considerations, and underlying pul- 37

monary disease. The final decision to extubate at case conclusion rested on both pre-specified criteria and provider 38

discretion. Relevant factors included airway stability, normothermia (core temperature ≥35 °C), hemostasis, CPB du- 39

ration, metabolic status (ideally pH >7.30 and PaCO2 ≤50 mmHg), and other elements such as level of conscious- 40

ness and adequacy of analgesia. 41

Data were prospectively collected from electronic medical records for patients extubated in the operating room be- 42

tween November 1, 2024, and June 30, 2025. Variables included demographic, preoperative, and intraoperative char- 43

acteristics. Postoperative outcomes were obtained from the EMR and supplemented with standardized outcomes 44

from the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) Adult Cardiac Surgery Database. Monthly case volumes and length of 45

stay were provided by the Department of Cardiac Surgery at MGH. 46

Descriptive statistics and baseline plots were generated in R (version 2025.05.1+513). Categorical variables are sum- 47

marized as frequency (percentage), and continuous variables as median [Q1, Q3] based on visual inspection and 48

quantitive 49

The use of these data for research was approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board, which 50

waived the need for informed consent. 51

RESULTS 52

Of 628 elective cardiac surgical cases requiring CPB, 171 patients (27%) were extubated in the operating room. The 53

monthly extubation rate averaged 29 (8.7)% (Figure 1A). Patients had a median age of 62 [54, 69] years and low 54

prevalences of major comorbidities (Table 1). Median CPB and cross-clamp times were 127 [93, 172] and 92 [67, 55

124] minutes, respectively. Seven patients (4.1%) underwent deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA) and 7 (4.1%) 56

underwent redo sternotomy. Aortic valve replacement, with or without concomitant aortic procedures, was the most 57

common operation (30% of ORE patients) and had the highest extubation rate (73% of all AVR cases; Figure 2). In- 58

traoperatively, patients received a median of 20 [20, 40] morphine milligram equivalents of hydromorphone and 72% 59

of patients received midazolam before CPB. At CPB end, 60% of patients required ≤1 vasopressor/inotrope; at extu- 60

bation this proportion increased to 82%. Fewer than 10% required ≥3 agents at either time point. 61

The median interval from procedure end to OR exit was 30 [22–41] minutes. Five patients (2.9%) were reintubated; 4 62

in the OR and 1 in the ICU (Supplemental Table 1). Seventeen patients (9.9%) were placed on bilevel positive airway 63

pressure (BiPAP) in the ICU, with use declining from 19% in November to 5% in June (Figure 3). All patients survived 64

to 30 days. 65

Median ICU length of stay was 25.5 [21.2, 45.6] hours for the ORE cohort versus 38.2 [23.3, 67.9] hours for the over- 66

all cohort, and median hospital length of stay was 5 [4, 7] days for both the ORE and overall cohorts (Figure 1B). ICU 67

and hospital LOS among ORE patients varied slightly by procedure (Figure 4). 68

DISCUSSION 69

Implementation of a protocol to consider ORE for all elective cardiac surgical patients was feasible, with a consistent 70

monthly extubation rate of approximately 30% across a range of procedures, including complex operations such as 71

Ross, DHCA, redo sternotomy, and congenital operations. Safety outcomes were favorable, with 0% 30-day mortality 72

and a low reintubation rate (2.9%). BiPAP use in the ICU declined over time, suggesting improved patient selection 73

and peri-extubation management. 74

Patients who were extubated in the OR were relatively young (median 62 years) and had low burden of major comor- 75

bid conditions (<10% for each), reflecting substantial provider discretion in patient selection. This subjectivity limits 76

causal inference from retrospective comparative analyses, as many determinants of extubation candidacy are incom- 77

pletely captured in clinical or national databases. The shorter ICU length of stay observed in this ORE cohort is there- 78

fore diﬀicult to interpret given confounding by patient selection. Importantly, patient selection inherently reflects clini- 79

cal judgement, and it remains essential that ORE be reserved for appropriate candidates, ideally within the framework 80

of a well-defined protocol. 81

Future analyses will employ rigorous causal inference methods to assess the eﬀicacy of our ORE protocol implemen- 82

tation, but these observational approaches remain inherently limited. A large, multi-center randomized clinical trial— 83

already in active planning—is required to determine whether, and in which populations, ORE provides clinical benefit, 84

with interim findings directly informing its design, patient selection, and implementation. 85
